orders.rationale: Both answers are accurate. A gets the July 2 vote, the July 4 declaration and the Treaty of Paris date right, but it is thin and calling 1783 the "establishment" muddies things. B is also accurate (signing began August 2, Constitution adopted 1787, ratified 1788, government running in 1789). It explains why "creation" has more than one date, and its sources fit its claims.

A is accurate on July 4, 1776, signing on August 2, the 1783 Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution dates (1787, 1788, 1789). It also explains how the nation's founding differs from its current government. B is correct and adds the July 2 vote, but it leaves out the Constitution. Its sources are vague, and it cites five but uses only [1].

A says Trump was president in 2016, which is false, and it contradicts itself with his January 2017 inauguration. Its sources don't support its main claim. B correctly names Obama as president for all of 2016 and clarifies that Trump won in November 2016 but took office in 2017. B is accurate, sourced and concise.

A is correct: Obama was president for all of 2016, and it notes that Trump won the election but took office in 2017. B wrongly names Trump as the 2016 president and contradicts itself by giving his January 2017 inauguration date. Its sources don't support the main claim.

A gets key facts wrong. Augustus founded the Principate in 27 BC, not 284 AD, and the 395 split did not "formally dissolve" the empire. It also contradicts itself and never states a length. B gives accurate dates and correct durations (about 500, 1,480 and 2,200 years) and explains how each one is counted.

A gives accurate durations: about 500 years for the West (27 BC–AD 476), about 1,480 years through 1453, and about 2,200 years counting from 753 BC. It explains each way of counting clearly. B never states a length. It wrongly dates Augustus's Principate to AD 284 and contradicts its own 27 BC start. It also misdescribes the 395 split as a formal dissolution.

B is accurate and complete. It names Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis, Morrow and Paine and explains what each did. A calls Strauss the primary designer, which is misleading. It also never gives Ellis's full name and leaves out Morrow, the architect behind the towers and the color. B also notes that Ellis's role was recognized in 2007.

A is accurate and complete: Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis (fired 1931, credited 2007), Morrow and Paine. Its one flaw: Moisseiff championed deflection theory but didn't invent it. B misleadingly says Strauss "primarily designed" the bridge, then contradicts that. B also omits Morrow and Paine and gives Ellis no first name.

B handles the ambiguous question by covering Chinese gunpowder rockets, Goddard's 1926 flight (details correct), the V-2's 1944 flight to space and Vostok 1/Korolev, all correctly sourced. A gets Goddard right but overstates him as building the first "practical rocket ship," leaves out the Chinese origins and cites an irrelevant novel.

A correctly explains the ambiguity and covers Chinese origins, Goddard (1926, accurate details), the V-2 reaching space in 1944 and the crewed Vostok 1/Korolev. B is accurate on Goddard but calls his rocket the first practical "rocket ship," skips Chinese origins and is less complete. It also lists an irrelevant novel as a source.

A's facts are correct, but it never says what the revolution was trying to achieve. It gives only dates and its legacy, and cites unused sources. B answers the question directly and accurately: ending the Ancien Régime, Enlightenment principles, the motto, the August decrees, and constitutional monarchy, then how the goals turned more radical. B is clearly better.

A answers the question directly and accurately. It covers ending the Ancien Régime, Enlightenment ideals, the motto, the early reforms and how the goals grew more radical. Its dates and events are correct. B's facts are true, but it never says what the goal was; it only describes when the Revolution began and ended. It also lists sources it never uses, including one on 1848.

Both answers are accurate. A is thin: it skips Franklin, Volta and Maxwell and only names Edison and Tesla for practical use. B gives a well-structured history from Thales, Gilbert and Gray through Franklin, Volta, Faraday and Maxwell. It also separates discovery from application and ends with a clear verdict. Some of B's claims, such as Maxwell's, are uncited but well established.

A is accurate and thorough: Gilbert's De Magnete (1600), Franklin, Volta's battery (1800), Faraday's induction (1831) and Maxwell. It gives a clear, sourced answer and separates the science from Edison and Tesla's practical work. B is correct but thin. It names only Gilbert, Faraday, Edison and Tesla, leaving out Franklin and Volta.

B directly explains why green never peaks and also covers violet. Its "10 times" figure is a bit high (blue vs. red is about 6x) and the ozone claim is debatable. A is correct but thin on the green part and lists unrelated sources (language, night sky).

A explains that Rayleigh scattering increases steadily toward shorter wavelengths, so nothing makes green peak. It also covers why the sky isn't violet and how the cones read the mix as pale blue. Its claims are accurate and grounded. B is correct but shallow: it never really answers 'why not green' and lists sources it doesn't use.

B is better. It explains why the coil turns (the Lorentz force) and how the commutator keeps it spinning in one direction. It also covers brushless and induction motors and the gasoline-engine meaning of "motor." A is accurate but shallow: it lists parts without explaining continuous rotation, and it cites two sources it never uses.

A explains the mechanism accurately: the Lorentz force, why the coil turns, and how the commutator keeps it spinning. It also covers brushless and induction motors and points out that "motor" could mean a combustion engine. B is correct but shallow. It leaves out the commutator, so it never explains why the motor keeps turning, and it lists sources it never cites.

B explains slicing and the main methods (FDM, SLA, SLS) accurately, with sources that match each topic. A is correct but vague. It gives no slicer or method detail, uses a dated 2019 framing, has awkward wording and lists an uncited source [5]. B is clearly more complete and more useful.

A explains the whole workflow accurately: the CAD model, slicing, and building layer by layer. It also covers how FDM, SLA and SLS each form a layer, and its claims fit its sources. B is accurate but thin. It never says how a layer is actually made, and its "as of 2019" note is dated. A is clearly better.

B actually explains how planes go fast: jet thrust, lift carrying the weight so engines only fight drag, thin air at cruise altitude, and drag rising near Mach 1. Its numbers are accurate. A barely explains anything. It gives the X-43 as both Mach 9.7 and 9.6 and overstates the mph. It also wrongly implies most planes fly supersonic or hypersonic.

A explains why planes are fast: thrust balancing drag, lift carrying the weight, thin air at altitude, and the sharp drag rise near Mach 1. Its figures are accurate. B wrongly says planes are fast because they're built for supersonic or hypersonic flight, gives the X-43 as both Mach 9.7 and 9.6, files it under Mach 10–25, and explains little.

A says IARC's 2B rating rested on "725 people with electromagnetic hypersensitivity." That's false; it came from brain-tumour studies. A also adds irrelevant Wi-Fi facts and misses key evidence. B accurately covers where the concern comes from (IARC, NTP rat study, 2026 policy changes), the stronger evidence (WHO review, physics, hypersensitivity trials) and open questions, all sourced.

A is accurate: it covers IARC 2B, the NTP rat study, the 2024 WHO-commissioned review, the physics, and the EHS provocation trials, with sources supporting each claim. B wrongly says the IARC classification rested on 725 people with electromagnetic hypersensitivity. It also adds irrelevant filler about Bluetooth range and gives thin evidence.

B is better. It rightly says government developed gradually, and its history (Neolithic Revolution, Sumer, kingship) is accurate. It also names the first theorists, Plato and Aristotle. A wrongly starts the idea with the Greeks and focuses on modern philosophers (Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke). It ignores government's far older existence and confuses theory with origin.

A is accurate and answers both readings of the question: government arose gradually after the Neolithic Revolution, with Sumer often named first, and the Greeks first theorized it. B wrongly implies government began with Greek and later thinkers, ignoring that it existed long before them. B also lists philosophers without much context, so it is less complete and less useful.

B explains the actual mechanisms accurately: resistive elements versus gas burners, thermostat cycling, the three ways heat transfers, convection fans and microwaves. It has only small simplifications. A is accurate but vague. It describes what an oven is more than how it works, and it gives little real mechanism.

A covers the full mechanism: electric resistance elements, gas burners, the thermostat cycling on and off, the three ways food heats, convection fans and microwaves. Its one slip is minor: it says infrared heats the air, when it mainly heats surfaces. B is vague and generic. It skips the heating mechanism and thermostat and adds an unneeded industrial aside, so it barely answers 'how'.

B is accurate and fuller. It covers families, snout, teeth, salt glands, where they live (two alligator species, South Florida overlap) and colour. A is mostly correct, but it names a subfamily after saying "different families", which is muddled. A also leaves out teeth, range and colour. Both are clear, but B gives more useful ways to tell them apart.

A is accurate and covers more: snout, teeth, salt glands, range, coexistence in South Florida and color. B is correct but thinner. It says "different families", then gives alligators a subfamily (their family is Alligatoridae). It skips teeth and range, though it usefully notes crocodiles are more aggressive. A is more complete and precise.

A gets the rosettes wrong: it says the leopard has spots inside its rosettes, which actually describes the jaguar, and then contradicts itself. It never describes the cheetah's coat or tear lines and pads with useless facts like chromosome count. B accurately covers coat, tear lines, build, range and black panthers, and is easy to use.

A is accurate and practical: cheetah spots vs. rosettes, rosette centres, tear lines, build and range. B wrongly gives leopard rosettes inner spots, contradicting its own jaguar point. It omits cheetah tear lines and solid spots. It pads with chromosome counts, gestation and lifespan, which don't help tell the cats apart.

B is better. It covers the central differences accurately: the Vedas, atman versus anatta, Brahman and God versus dependent arising, and caste. It also notes that short comparisons simplify. A skips the core doctrinal differences. It uses peripheral points like follower counts, a questionable claim about conversion, and the misleading labels "state religion" and "subclass."

A is accurate and well sourced on the main doctrinal differences: atman vs. anatta, Brahman/God, the Vedas and caste. B skips those, wrongly calls Hinduism "a state religion" and treats both being Indian religions as a difference. Its conversion and follower-count points are minor. A is clearly better.

Both answers are accurate. A explains the core difference correctly but briefly, and it lists sources [4] and [5] without citing them. B adds useful practical points: examples of acidic ingredients, double-acting powder, when recipes use both, and why you can't swap them one-for-one. B's final paragraph has no citation, but it is common knowledge. B is more complete and more useful.

Both are accurate. A is more complete: it covers double-acting powder, why recipes use both leaveners (with an example) and swapping cautions. Its swap and taste claims have no source, a small grounding gap. B is correct but thin, skipping double-acting powder and practical use. It lists two sources it never uses.

Both answers correctly say the Mongol Empire was much bigger. A gives a very precise Roman figure of 5,957,000 km² that is doubtful; about 5 million km² is the usual estimate. Its source list is also padded with duplicates. B gives accurate, well-sourced context: Trajan's peak, Hadrian's withdrawal, populations, and the British Empire comparison. That context helps without padding the answer.

Both say the Mongol Empire was larger. A adds dates, population, Rome's peak under Trajan and the British Empire comparison, with mostly standard figures. Its 12,000 km span looks overstated. B is bare, gives no dates and uses an unusual, unexplained 5,957,000 km² Roman figure with vague sources.

Both answers are correct: espresso has more caffeine per ounce, drip more per serving. B adds the double-shot comparison, per-ounce figures and a note on variability. A's 115–175 mg for 240 ml is high next to the common ~95 mg figure, and its source may give that range for a smaller cup. B is more complete and nuanced.

Both are accurate: espresso has more caffeine per ounce, but a normal cup of drip has more in total. A adds per-ounce figures, a double-shot comparison and a note that amounts vary. B is correct and concise, but its 115–175 mg cup estimate runs high against the usual ~95 mg, and it skips the double-shot comparison.

B explains the structure of each (a bacterium is a full cell; a virus is genetic material in a capsid), why antibiotics fail, and what treats viruses instead. A's definitions are vague and miss the fact that viruses aren't cells. It cites sources that don't match its claims and adds an irrelevant point about how bacteria fight off viruses (CRISPR).

A is more accurate and covers both parts of the question. It explains what bacteria and viruses are made of, why antibiotics can't affect viruses, and what treats viral infections instead. B describes the difference only vaguely, mixes up its source numbers, and adds an off-topic, muddled point about CRISPR. That makes B less grounded and less useful.

A gets the key difference wrong. Linux permissions are not "static" next to "dynamic" Windows ones. A also mixes up AGDLP, a way of organising Active Directory groups, with the NTFS permission model. B accurately covers owner/group/other and the special bits, how Windows reads ACL entries in order, inheritance, the null vs empty list case, and POSIX ACLs. B is better grounded and more useful.

A is accurate throughout: owner/group/others order, setuid/setgid/sticky, NTFS allow/deny entries, inheritance, audit list, null vs empty list, POSIX ACLs. B is shallow. It treats AGDLP, an Active Directory practice, as core to file permissions. Its "static vs dynamic" contrast is misleading, since Linux also assigns permissions by group.

Both are accurate. B covers more: Luther meant to reform the Church, not leave it, and taught salvation by faith alone. It also gives correct dated events: excommunication in January 1521, the Diet of Worms, and the 1534 German Bible. A is correct and grounded but thinner and never says he didn't intend a split.

A is accurate: the 1517 Theses on indulgences, faith alone, the January 1521 excommunication, the Edict of Worms and the 1534 Bible. It also says Luther meant reform, not schism. B is correct but thinner and repetitive. It misses the reform-not-schism point and lists sources it never uses.

A says the technology behind AI is "artificial intelligence itself." That answer is circular and fails the main question, though its Dartmouth 1956 facts are right. B correctly names the programmable digital computer and adds accurate, sourced details: Hanover, the organizers, McCarthy coining the term in 1955, and Logic Theorist. B answers both parts clearly.

A correctly names the programmable digital computer and Dartmouth (1956), with accurate details on organizers, the 1955 coinage and Logic Theorist. B says AI's founding technology is "AI itself", which is circular and doesn't answer the technology part. Only B's Dartmouth and Logic Theorist facts are correct.

Both answers correctly say the Danube flows through Budapest and empties into the Black Sea, and both cite sources. B adds accurate details: Buda and Pest, the roughly 28 km stretch through the city, the Black Forest source, the river's length and the delta. None of that was asked for. A answers more briefly, which suits a phone. Neither is clearly better.

Both are correct and complete: the Danube flows through Budapest into the Black Sea. A adds accurate, sourced extras (Buda/Pest split, about 2,850 km, delta on the Romania–Ukraine border) that the question didn't ask for. B answers equally accurately and more concisely. Neither is clearly better.

B correctly names Spanish as Peru's main language and gives accurate context on Quechua and Aymara. Calling them "three official languages" simplifies things slightly: Quechua and Aymara are official where they predominate. A never mentions Spanish and focuses only on Quechua, which misleads on the main question. It also pads its source list with sources it doesn't use.

A gets it right: Cusco is in Peru, where Spanish is the main language, and it adds Quechua and Aymara with about-right percentages. It slightly overstates Quechua and Aymara as official nationwide. B never mentions Spanish, so its true Quechua claims mislead. Its Inca-only sources don't back its claim about today's speakers.

A is wrong: it names Edward VII, whose own stated reign (1901–1910) began after 1889, so the answer contradicts itself. Its reasoning about the George VI source is also confused. B correctly names Queen Victoria (reigned 1837–1901) and the March 1889 completion date, with relevant sources and accurate extra context. B is clearly better.

A is right: the tower was finished in March 1889, during Queen Victoria's reign (1837–1901), and its supporting details are accurate and backed by sources. B is wrong. It names Edward VII even though his own stated reign dates (1901–1910) begin after 1889, so it contradicts itself, and its sources don't support that claim.

B correctly names Oxford (Queen's College, 1973–76, first-class physics), and its extra details match his known biographies. A never says Oxford and lists Emanuel School, a secondary school, as if it answered the question. Its Southampton remark is about where he later worked, so it doesn't help.

A gives the correct answer: The Queen's College, Oxford (1973–76), with a first-class physics degree. Its extra details are accurate and sourced. B never names Oxford and lists Emanuel School, which is a secondary school, as if it answered the university question. It also brings in Southampton, where he worked rather than studied, which confuses the answer.

Both answers correctly name Japan as the host and Mount Fuji as its tallest mountain. B also gives accurate supporting detail: 3,776 m, a stratovolcano on Honshu, and a UNESCO site. A is correct but bare, and its source list includes irrelevant entries (Mount Olympus, Mauna Kea). B is slightly more useful.

Both answers correctly name Japan (Tokyo 1964) and Mount Fuji. A also gets its extra details right: 3,776 m, an active stratovolcano on Honshu, a UNESCO site. A's sources fit its claims. B is correct but bare. It lists sources it never uses that have nothing to do with the question (Mount Olympus, Mauna Kea), which makes its citations look less trustworthy. A is somewhat better.

Both correctly say Cambodia uses the riel. A is accurate but leaves out that US dollars are widely used day to day, which matters for "what currency do they use." B adds accurate, well-sourced points: dollar use in Siem Reap, the stable exchange rate, riel given as change and the government's push for the riel. B is more complete and more practical.

Both correctly name the Cambodian riel. A also covers how widely US dollars are used, the stable exchange rate and tips on carrying riel, all supported by its sources, which makes it more useful. B is accurate but bare, and several of the sources it lists, such as the band, have nothing to do with the question.

A is accurate but generic. It never explains how printing actually spread ideas, and source [5] is listed but never cited. B gives specific, verifiable details: the Theses spread within weeks, Luther's edition counts, cheap Flugschriften pamphlets and reading aloud to people who couldn't read. It also covers the research linking printing presses to Protestant adoption and notes that scholars still debate it.

A answers directly with specific evidence: Theses spread in two weeks, about 300,000 copies, pamphlets read aloud, print-city studies. It notes the causal debate. Figures are plausible but unchecked. B is accurate but generic, with little evidence and vague sources. A is clearly more useful.

A is vague and muddled: it says he kept writing, treating sketches and letters as "evidence," which doesn't explain how he worked. It names only the Ninth Symphony. B is accurate: inner hearing, sketchbooks, conversation books, the 1798 onset and the 1802 Heiligenstadt Testament. It lists many later works, flags the rod-biting story as unverified, and stays clear.

A is accurate: deafness from about 1798, the 1802 Heiligenstadt Testament, inner hearing, sketchbooks and conversation books. It names many later works and labels the doubtful stories as such. B is vague and garbled: it says "sketches and letters as evidence" without explaining how he composed, names only the Ninth, and adds speculative framing.

B is better. Its figures are current and its maths is right: about 31 times for metropolitan France and about 26.6 times including overseas France. It also flags that the answer depends on which France you mean. A's 26.5 is valid but uses an outdated Russia figure, calls total areas "land areas", and ignores the metropolitan-versus-overseas question. B's "most people mean" claim is unsupported but minor.

A's ratios are right (≈31× mainland France, ≈26.6× with overseas regions), and it covers the ambiguity over which France is meant. B's 26.5× is roughly right but uses an older Russia figure and calls total area "land area". It also ignores metropolitan France and lists sources it never cites.

Both correctly say the Netherlands is about twice as dense. A's 480/km² fits neither the land-only (~540) nor the total-area (~430) basis and goes unexplained; its sources repeat. B gives both bases with consistent maths and credible sources. Its Destatis figure of 240 is a bit high (actual ~234) but immaterial. B is clearer and more accurate.

Both answer yes and say how much. A is better: its land-area (~541/km²) and total-area (~436/km²) figures check out arithmetically, the ratios are consistent, and it explains the water-area ambiguity. Germany's 240/km² is slightly high (~234–237), but close. B's Dutch figure of 480/km² matches neither standard measure, and its sources are vague.

Both answers give the correct figure of about 1.3 million Earths by volume. A starts with the Sun's mass, which is true but has nothing to do with how much fits inside, so the reasoning reads muddled. B explains the volume calculation clearly. It also notes that solid spheres pack at about 74%, giving roughly 960,000 whole Earths, and its sources support this.

A gives the correct 1.3 million by volume, explains the 109³ math, and adds the packing point (about 74%, so roughly 960,000 whole Earths). B gets 1.3 million right, but it opens with the Sun's mass, which is true but irrelevant and possibly confusing. B also skips the packing point, so it is less complete and less clear.

Both get ~4,240 hours (~177 days nonstop). A has a logic error: "roughly 6 months if you include rest" is wrong, since 6 months is already the nonstop time. A also says 21,195 km instead of 21,196. B uses the correct official figure, adds a realistic 8-hours-a-day estimate (~530 days) and the Ming-wall alternative, and its maths is correct.

A uses the correct official length (21,196 km) and gives accurate times nonstop and at 8 h/day. It adds the Ming-wall option and terrain caveats. B is close on length, but it wrongly says about 6 months includes rest, when 176 days is the nonstop time. B also lists sources it never cites and leaves out the definitional nuance.

Both answers get about 4,043 m from 8,848.86 m minus 4,805.59 m, which is correct. A's sources for the alternative heights (8,840 m and 4,807.3 m) are weak, mixed-up citations. B gives dates for both measurements, explains why Mont Blanc's ice cap changes height, and says it couldn't find the 2025 survey result. That makes B better grounded.

Both answers correctly compute 8,848.86 − 4,805.59 = 4,043.27 m. A is better because it dates both surveys, explains why Mont Blanc's height changes and admits it found no official 2025 figure. B suggests Everest is "sometimes listed as 8,840 m", which seems to be an old historical figure rather than a current alternative. B also gives no survey dates.

B answers the question correctly with sourced support: the CDC says Mexico's tap water isn't safe, and B explains how it gets contaminated in pipes and storage tanks, then gives practical advice. A never answers. It treats ozone, an air pollutant, as if it bore on water safety, and its 'Metropolitan Water Authority' claim has no source behind it.

A gives a clear, correct answer: don't drink the tap water. It cites the CDC and explains that contamination happens in pipes and storage tanks after treatment. It also gives practical tips, though the claim about ice at restaurants has no source. B never answers the question, and it uses air-ozone pollution as if it were evidence about water, which misleads. B is not useful.

B answers directly and correctly: no tipping, service charges at upscale places, otoshi/seating fees, and saying thanks instead. Its sources are about tipping and back up its claims. A is honest that its sources don't cover tipping, but it hides the correct answer at the end and gives no detail. B is clearly the more useful answer.

Answer A says clearly that you don't tip, and covers service charges, otoshi and seating fees, and how to show thanks, all backed by relevant sources. Answer B spends most of its length on sources that don't address tipping. It is honest about that gap, but its short general-knowledge answer is unsupported and thin.

A says rinsing with fresh water is fine, but fresh water can make stinging cells fire more venom. It also leaves out hot-water immersion, the main recommended pain treatment. B is accurate and matches ILCOR and Red Cross guidance: rinse with seawater, remove tentacles safely, use heat for pain, take a species-specific approach to vinegar, and know the emergency warning signs. B is also clear and practical.

A is correct and practical: seawater rinse, no fresh water, hot water for pain, vinegar depends on species, clear emergency signs. B wrongly says fresh water is fine for rinsing and leaves out heat for pain, the most useful step. B also relies on general jellyfish articles rather than first-aid guidance.

B is accurate. It gives khop khun and khor thot, notes that khor thot also means "sorry," and explains the khrap/kha polite particles and how to pronounce them. A gets the basic words right but uses the odd romanization "khub khun." It also wrongly calls ขอบคุณ the most formal form (that is ขอบพระคุณ), leaves out the particles, and cites sources that barely relate to its claims.

A is accurate and complete: it covers the khrap/kha particles, what "khor thot" is used for, and pronunciation. Calling the "khop" vowel short is a small slip; it is long. B wrongly calls ขอบคุณ the most formal form (ขอบพระคุณ is), leaves out the particles, repeats itself, and cites sources that don't clearly support it.

B is accurate, specific and well sourced. It covers symptoms, when they start, HACE/HAPE warning signs, Peru details (Cusco 3,400 m, Dead Woman's Pass 4,215 m, Sacred Valley) and concrete ascent rules. A repeats itself, omits the severe warning signs and Cusco, and cites no source for its prevention advice.

A is accurate and covers both parts: mild AMS and dangerous HACE/HAPE warning signs, Cusco and Inca Trail elevations, ascent rules, and Diamox. B is generic and repeats itself, gives no Peru details beyond one altitude, skips the severe warning signs, and over-simplifies by saying to descend at any symptom.

A presents Norwegian polar night and midnight sun dates (Andenes) as if they apply to Iceland, which is misleading and misuses its sources. It also gives no practical timing. B accurately gives the season (late Sep–early Apr), the best months, the 9pm–2am window and viewing tips, all grounded in relevant Iceland sources.

A gives an accurate season (late September to early April), explains when activity peaks around the equinoxes and the best hours of the night, and offers practical tips. B uses polar-night and midnight-sun dates from Norway (Nordland/Andenes) as if they applied to Iceland. It also wrongly says winter is when aurora activity is highest, and it gives no months or tips.

B gives an accurate two-day plan grouped by area and backed by itinerary sources, with good tips on avoiding crowds. A's festival dates are right (Jidai Matsuri is today), but it leaves out Fushimi Inari and Arashiyama and has no day plan. It also wrongly says two days covers only one or two highlights, and its general sources don't support the itinerary.

A gives an accurate two-day plan grouped by area, plus sound tips on avoiding crowds at Fushimi Inari, backed by relevant sources. B's festival dates are right, but it gives no day-by-day structure, leaves out Fushimi Inari and Arashiyama, pads with Kyoto Tower, and assumes the trip can be timed around festivals. Its sources are vague.

A misreads its sources: the polio proof rule applies to travellers leaving Kenya, not arriving. It also leaves out yellow fever, hepatitis A, typhoid and malaria pills. B matches CDC guidance on yellow fever (both the entry rule and the recommendation), routine shots, situational vaccines and malaria. It is clear and practical, and says it couldn't check Kenya's Ministry of Health page.

A matches CDC guidance on yellow fever entry rules, routine and recommended vaccines, and malaria, and it admits what it couldn't verify. B reverses the polio rule: Kenya-origin travelers need proof when leaving, not visitors arriving. B also omits yellow fever, hepatitis A and typhoid, and wrongly claims nothing else is needed.

A is accurate but vague: no actionable rules, and it lists unrelated sources ("Mind", "Keep"). B correctly covers Scottish, English/Welsh and Dartmoor law and Leave No Trace specifics. But it invents a persona ("Where I live in Scotland") and calls the written two-or-three-night limit "unwritten". B is still far more useful.

A is accurate and specific on access law (Scotland, England and Wales, the 2025 Dartmoor ruling) and Leave No Trace basics. But it falsely says "where I live in Scotland," and the 2–3 night limit is in the written code, not an unwritten rule. B is vague and generic, cites meaningless sources and gives no actionable advice.

A gives a sound list of foods to feed but misses key toxic items: avocado, chocolate, caffeine and onion. Its claims about flour and soaked bread are shaky, and it never uses source [2]. B is accurate and well sourced, covers both parts of the question in depth, and notes that its toxic list comes from pet-bird guidance. Some simplifications are minor.

A is accurate and thorough. It covers safe wild-bird foods and key toxic foods (avocado, chocolate, caffeine, salt, onion, xylitol), with sensible caveats, so it beats B. B suggests "flour", which is odd advice, and skips the major toxic foods. Its "avoid" list is thin, so it is less complete and less useful.

A says its sources don't cover the question, then offers only "lubricate the pivots" and pads it with forced links to unrelated sources (beveled edges, hand guards). B gives accurate, practical steps from relevant sources: a quick spray, then removing, cleaning and greasing the pin, tightening screws, or replacing the hinge. It also warns against pulling all the pins at once. B is clearly better.

A gives accurate, well-sourced steps, from a quick spray to pulling and greasing the pin, plus a safety warning and backup fixes. B admits its sources don't cover the question, which is honest. But it offers only a vague lubricant tip and stretches irrelevant sources, such as hand guards and beveled door edges, to look supported. A is clearly better.

B gives a usable day-by-day method with amounts, a timeline, troubleshooting and readiness signs. It is sourced, though 26–29°C is slightly warm. A is vague and somewhat misleading: it leaves the mix for days before feeding, conflates a starter with a sponge and calls for a "firm" starter. It has no quantities or readiness checks and does little for a beginner.

Answer A is better. It gives a practical, accurate method with amounts, a feeding schedule, the right temperature, troubleshooting for the day 2–4 slump and clear signs the starter is ready, all supported by its sources.
